passage: By the time the sun climbed over the wheat, Kamal had swept the yard, fed the buffaloes and finished two chapters of homework. His mother Rukmini watched him from the doorway, holding her tea. "You're up early. Again." "Just helping, Ma." He kept sweeping. All week he had been doing this. Under it sat a small hard thought: if he hadn't argued so much with his brother, if he had scored better in maths, maybe his parents wouldn't be splitting up. Rukmini set down her tea and sat on the step. "Kamal, come here. Your father and I have talked. Nothing you did caused this. Nothing." His broom slowed. His shoulders shook. "You can love us both, and you don't have to be perfect for us."

qa.q: What had Kamal finished before sunrise?
qa.a: He had swept the yard, fed the buffaloes and finished two chapters of homework.

qa.q: What secret thought was Kamal carrying under all his chores?
qa.a: He wondered whether his arguments with his brother or his maths marks had caused his parents' split, which made him try to be perfect.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do that helped Kamal, and what could he do next?
qa.a: She told him plainly that nothing he did caused it. He can keep loving both parents and let the chores go back to normal, instead of trying to fix them by behaving perfectly.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel seeing her son work so hard all week?
qa.a: Probably worried and sad, since the extra chores told her Kamal was carrying something heavy, and she chose to answer it with plain, clear words.

grounding: Shows a teen secretly wondering if his fights or grades caused his parents' split, trying to be perfect, and hearing plainly that it was not his fault.

passage:
Every morning that week, Leila made her bed before her alarm went off. She ironed her school shirt, finished her homework on the tram, and brought home a spelling test with full marks, which she left carefully on the kitchen table in their Lyon apartment.
Her father, Marek, noticed. On Thursday he found her scrubbing the bathroom sink at ten at night.
"Leila. What's going on?"
She kept scrubbing. "If I don't argue, and my grades are good, maybe Maman will come back."
Marek sat on the edge of the bath. The next evening Maman came over, and the three of them sat at the kitchen table.
"We are separating because of us," Maman said slowly. "Not because of your grades, not because of any fight you had with anyone. Nothing you did."
"Nothing," Marek repeated. "You can stop being perfect. We both love you exactly the same."
Leila put her head down on the table and finally cried.

qa.q: Where did Leila leave her spelling test?
qa.a: On the kitchen table in their Lyon apartment.

qa.q: Why was Leila scrubbing the sink so late at night?
qa.a: She felt guilty and secretly feared her arguments or grades caused the split, so she was anxiously trying to be perfect to bring Maman back.

qa.q: What did the parents do well here?
qa.a: They noticed the perfect behaviour, came together and told Leila plainly that the separation was not her fault and that they both still love her.

qa.q: What is it like for Marek when he finds Leila cleaning at ten at night?
qa.a: He seems worried and saddened; he sits down beside her instead of scolding, realising she is carrying a burden that is not hers.

grounding: A teen secretly fears she caused her parents' split and tries to be perfect until both parents tell her plainly it is not her fault.

passage:
Madhav had been in the counsellor's room three times this term, always saying he was "just tired." Ms Anjali, the school counsellor, had noticed his marks dropping and then, strangely, his homework becoming neat and early.
On Wednesday he finally said it. "My parents fought about my maths tuition fees. Two months later, Papa moved out. So."
Ms Anjali did not rush to disagree. "That's a heavy thing to carry alone. Would you let me invite both of them in, so you can hear it from them?"
On Friday afternoon, Madhav's mother and father sat side by side on the small sofa, stiff but present.
"Beta, this is between your mother and me," his father said. "It started years before your tuition."
"You did not cause this," his mother said. "We both love you. That doesn't change."
Madhav stared at the carpet, then nodded. His shoulders dropped for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What did Madhav's parents fight about, according to him?
What had Madhav been feeling that made him say he was 'just tired'?
qa.a: He felt guilty, secretly believing the fight over his tuition fees had caused his father to move out.

qa.q: How did Ms Anjali support Madhav wisely?
qa.a: She listened without rushing to argue, named how heavy the feeling was, and brought both parents in so he could hear the truth from them.

qa.q: How might Madhav's parents see this meeting?
qa.a: They probably feel awkward and sad sitting together, but they come because they want their son to know clearly that the split is not his fault.

grounding: A teen who wonders if he caused his parents' separation hears from both parents plainly, in the counsellor's room, that it was not his fault.
